Admissions

Questions to ask before primary-school enrolment.

The best school visit is a conversation, not a presentation. Thoughtful questions help families understand what daily life will actually be like for their child.

By Princeway CollegePublished 6 November 20267 minute read

Admissions conversations often focus on whether a place is available and what it costs. Those answers are essential, but enrolment is also the right time to understand how the school teaches, communicates and cares for children.

Keep a short list on your phone or in a notebook. You do not need to ask every question below. Choose the ones that matter most for your child and family, and listen for specific examples rather than perfect-sounding promises.

Questions about learning

  • Which curriculum and teaching medium are used for my child’s grade?
  • What does a typical day or week include?
  • How do teachers check whether children understand a lesson?
  • How are reading, writing, speaking and numeracy developed?
  • What happens when a child needs more time or further challenge?
  • How much homework is normally given, and what support is expected from parents?

If the school teaches in English, ask how children with different levels of confidence are supported. A useful answer should explain classroom practice: visual support, modelling, guided talk, vocabulary development or small-group work.

Questions about wellbeing and behaviour

  • How do you help new children settle during the first weeks?
  • How are classroom expectations taught?
  • What happens when children argue, exclude someone or repeatedly disrupt learning?
  • Who does a child approach when worried or unwell?
  • How and when are parents contacted about a concern?

Listen for a balance of boundaries and support. Children need clear limits, but discipline should also help them understand impact, repair relationships and learn a better response.

Questions about teachers and classes

Ask who will teach the class, how responsibilities are shared and whom parents contact first. Class size is useful information, but it is not the only measure of attention. Ask how the teacher organises the room, monitors work and notices a child who rarely asks for help.

You can also ask how staff development is handled and how consistency is maintained when a teacher is absent or changes during the year.

A school’s quality is often clearest in the systems used on an ordinary Tuesday—not only in its special events or best photographs.

Questions about communication with families

  • How will I receive notices and progress information?
  • How often are parent–teacher conversations held?
  • How can I arrange a private discussion?
  • What response time should families expect?
  • How does the school prefer parents to raise a disagreement or complaint?

A healthy system protects teachers from constant interruption while giving parents a reliable way to communicate. Ask what information must be shared immediately and what can wait for an appointment.

Questions about daily arrangements

  • What are the exact arrival and collection times?
  • What identification or authorisation is required at collection?
  • What meals, snacks, books, stationery and uniforms are needed?
  • How are allergies, medication and emergency contacts managed?
  • Which activities happen outside the regular timetable?
  • Are transport services available, or are families responsible for all travel?

Visit the route during normal traffic. A daily journey that appears simple on a quiet weekend may feel very different on a school morning.

Questions about fees and commitments

Ask for the full current fee information in writing. Clarify registration, term or monthly fees, materials, uniforms, activities, transport, deposits and notice periods. If an item is optional, ask how opting out affects the child’s day.

Avoid making assumptions from an old social-media post or a fee quoted to another family. Programmes and costs can change.

What to observe while you are there

Notice whether adults greet children, whether instructions are calm and whether the environment appears organised for the age group. Look at student work: does it show variety and thought, or does every piece look identical? Listen to the way staff speak about children who need support.

Your child’s reaction matters, but a shy or excited response during one visit is not a final verdict. Combine it with what you observed and what the school explained.

After the visit

Write down three things

  1. One clear strength of the school.
  2. One question that still needs an answer.
  3. One reason the environment may or may not suit your child.
